newsitem.title: USA: Juice is sweet success for Nantucket Nectars.
newsitem.headline: Juice is sweet success for Nantucket Nectars.

text.p: When Nantucket Nectars turns on the juice, profits flow with passion.
"We didn't start this to make money," said Tom Scott, who started Nantucket Nectars AllServe seven years ago with friend and fellow Brown University graduate Tom First.

"We entered this because we're passionate about the products," he said with the fervor only a young man in jeans and a T-shirt can convey. Jeans appear to be the preferred dress and dogs are also welcomed in the company's corporate headquarters in Cambridge, Mass.

The two 31-year-old entrepreneurs began what they expect to be a $60 million a year business in 1997 from the deck of a 22-foot Boston Whaler, bringing supplies and running errands for the owners of the multimillion-dollar yachts moored in Nantucket harbour for the summer.
"Working for yourself, outside on the water, is really good. It's the greatest job in the world," First said.
The pair would bring coffee, newspapers and laundry to the vessels. They even pumped out sewage. On the side, they waited tables and made money scalloping.
"We were working 14-, 16-hour days and not even knowing it," First said.

One night after work at their shack-turned-grocery-store on the end of a wharf, First tried to duplicate a peach drink he had tasted on a trip through Spain, using a blender to make batch after batch from canned peaches.
The "juice guys" -- as they began calling themselves -- sold the home-made beverage from the stern of the boat. The drink became a hit in the harbour.
Combining their savings of $20,000, they had just enough to produce 1,700 cases in a New York state bottling plant.
The drink sold out when they started to distribute it on Nantucket, neighbouring Martha's Vineyard and Cape Cod, but their profit was gobbled up by expenses.
"We filled every part of the cycle of failure," First said. "We made every mistake you could. We weren't doing it as a business. We were doing it as 23-, 24-year-old kids."
Their commitment to using real fruit juices and other quality ingrediants caught the attention of one boater -- Mike Egan, the founder of Alamo Rent-A-Car -- who helped back them.
"We used to clean his boat. He saw what we were doing and I think he had faith in us," Scott said.

The company, which still operates the shack, now has 100 employees. Its 32 products are distributed in 30 states. And, its owners still spend 14 to 16 hour days trying to improve everything they can about the juice.

"We believe in what we call the 'quality juice evolution solution' and that is why, when there is a lull in the rest of the industry, this company has doubled in size every year," Scott said. "We did $30 million in sales last year. We expect to do between $55 and $60 million this year."

Juices -- including the cartons of orange and grapefruit juices sold in supermarkets -- made up a $5.6 billion segment of the drink market, according to Joan Holleran at the trade publication Beverage Industry.
However, competition is fierce in the industry.
Quaker Oats Co., for example, was forced to sell its Snapple product line to Triac Cos., which markets Mystic brand fruit drinks, for $550 million. Quaker bought Snapple for $1.3 billion.
First and Scott are ever weary of repeating Snapple's mistakes and believe their "juice evolution solution" -- listening to customers and upgrading quality whenever possible -- will help.
"We're paranoid people," First said. "We never think that what we've created is good enough. We're always thinking of ways to improve the product, improve the marketing. improve the distribution.
"We're the juice guys. The products' real and so are we."
